overview.title: 📖 Overview: Threads, Snails, and When a Melacha Is Truly 'Finished'
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 75a–75b
overview.hebrewSource: הַמּוֹתֵחַ חוּט שֶׁל תְּפִירָה בְּשַׁבָּת חַיָּיב חַטָּאת
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens with three unrelated teachings Rav Zutra bar Toviya transmits in Rav's name — on tightening a loose stitch, on learning from a Persian magosh, and on the obligation to calculate astronomical seasons — before returning to the mishna's list of primary labors. It works through the ḥilazon (the dye-snail), trapping and slaughtering an animal, and salting and tanning a hide, in each case asking exactly which melacha, or how many, the act violates. It then gathers several 'finishing' actions under the single category of striking the final hammer blow, closes out the mishna's exclusions, and introduces a new mishna: an item is liable for being carried out of the house only if it is the kind of item people typically bother to store.

slides.title: 🧵 Tightening a Stitch, Learning from a Magosh, and the Stars
slides.subtitle: Three teachings Rav Zutra bar Toviya transmits in the name of Rav
slides.label: Rav's three rulings:
slides.text: One who TIGHTENS a stitching thread on Shabbat — pulling two separating parts of a garment back together — is liable to a sin-offering, since it is equivalent to sewing itself; just as, when a worm tore a curtain, people would tear it further so it could be sewn without the mend showing. One who learns even a single matter from a magosh (a Persian priest) is liable to death. And one who knows how to calculate astronomical seasons and constellations but does not — people should not even speak with him, for the Torah calls that calculation 'your wisdom and understanding in the eyes of the nations' (Deuteronomy 4:6). Rav and Shmuel disputed whether a magosh is a sorcerer or a heretic; since the Torah permits merely LEARNING about sorcery (only practicing it is forbidden), Rav's severe ruling proves he understood magosh as heretics.

slides.title: 🐚 Cracking Open a Ḥilazon — One Violation or Two?
slides.subtitle: Trapping the dye-snail, and whether cracking its shell is also 'threshing'

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: One who traps a ḥilazon (the snail used for sky-blue dye) and cracks its shell for the blood is liable to only ONE sin-offering.

lines.speaker: Rabbi Yehuda
lines.text: Liable to TWO — trapping, and also threshing! Extracting what he wants from its shell is the same act as threshing grain from its husk.

lines.speaker: The Rabbis
lines.text: No — threshing applies only to produce that GROWS from the ground, not to a creature's shell.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But cracking it open while it's alive kills it — shouldn't he also be liable for taking a life?

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: Exempt — he has no intent to kill it. He actually prefers it stay alive as long as possible, since dye from a live ḥilazon is finer. Since death works AGAINST his own interest, even Rabbi Shimon exempts him here.

callout.label: Rabbi Yoḥanan's alternative:
callout.text: Perhaps the whole question is moot — the case may simply be one where the ḥilazon was already dead before its shell was cracked.

slides.title: 🔨 Striking the Final Blow — Six 'Finishing' Acts
slides.subtitle: Rabba and Rabbi Zeira's rule: any act that completes a piece of work counts as makeh b'patish
rows: Rubbing a hide smooth between the pillars
Planing the tops of posts even
Cutting (in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's name)
Spreading a bandage onto a wound
Engraving a figure, or blowing glass into shape
Striking the final blow (Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish)
Removing loose threads from a cloak, if he insists on it

callout.label: Also on this daf:
callout.text: Writing one large letter where two could fit is exempt — only one letter was written. But ERASING one large letter to make room for two is liable: 'a greater stricture in erasing than in writing' (Rabbi Menaḥem, son of Rabbi Yosei).

slides.title: 🔪 Slaughtering and Salting — Which Melacha Applies?
slides.subtitle: Two disputes over what an act 'really' accomplishes

boxes.title: Slaughtering an Animal
items: Rav: liable for DYEING — a butcher wants the blood to pool visibly at the block, to draw customers to fresh meat
Shmuel: liable for TAKING A LIFE

boxes.title: Salting / Tanning a Hide
items: Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish: salting and tanning are really one labor — replace one with 'drafting' (marking cut-lines) to keep 39 distinct categories
Rabba bar Rav Huna: salting MEAT to preserve it is liable as tanning
Rava: there is no 'tanning' at all with regard to food

boxes.title: The Compromise
items: Rav Ashi: even Rabba bar Rav Huna meant only heavy salting to preserve meat for a journey — not ordinary salting to eat at home, since no one turns his own food into 'wood'

slides.title: 📦 A New Mishna: 'Fit to Store' Decides Who's Liable
slides.subtitle: Carrying an item into the public domain on Shabbat
headers: Who is liable for carrying it out?
rows: Anyone who carries it out — ordinary sin-offering liability
An item too insignificant to bother storing
Only someone who personally stored THAT item — his own act shows he values it

callout.label: Two views on 'not fit to store':
callout.text: Rav Pappa: the blood of a menstruating woman (though some hold it could still be saved to feed a cat). Mar Ukva: wood from a tree used for idol worship, which has no permitted value at all. Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina adds that this whole principle is NOT Rabbi Shimon's view — he holds the mishna's measures apply only to one who actually stored the item, regardless of common practice.

summary.principle: A prohibited labor is defined by its true functional result — what the act actually accomplishes and why a person would want it — so the same physical motion can fall under different melachot, or under none at all, depending on intent, context, and whether the result is truly desired or complete.

flowSteps.content: 🧵 Tightening a stitch = sewing; learning sorcery-theory from a magosh = forbidden only because Rav treats them as heretics
🐚🔪 Ḥilazon and slaughtering: liability tracks the desired RESULT (dye, or a bloodied block), not just the physical act

columns.content: 🔨 Many 'finishing touches' — smoothing, chiseling, trimming threads — all fall under striking the final blow
📦 Carrying liability depends on whether the item is the kind people typically store

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Shabbat liability follows the purpose and completeness of an act, not merely its outward motion

quiz.q: According to Rav, why is one who tightens a loose stitching thread on Shabbat liable to a sin-offering?
o: Because pulling thread is always considered weaving
Because reattaching two separating parts of a garment this way is equivalent to sewing itself
Because thread may not be touched on Shabbat at all
Because it counts as tying a permanent knot
quiz.e: Rav Zutra bar Toviya taught in Rav's name that tightening a stitch to rejoin separating fabric has the same effect as sewing, making one liable for the melacha of sewing.

quiz.q: What does Rav's ruling — that learning even one matter from a magosh incurs the death penalty — prove about how he understood the term 'magosh'?
o: That a magosh is simply a sorcerer, since the Torah forbids all sorcery
That a magosh is a heretic, since the Torah permits merely learning ABOUT sorcery (only practicing it is forbidden)
That a magosh is a type of judge
That the term has no special halakhic meaning
quiz.e: Since Deuteronomy is understood to permit studying sorcery in order to understand or teach it, Rav's total ban on learning from a magosh shows he considered them heretics rather than mere sorcerers.

quiz.q: Why does Rava exempt one who cracks open a LIVE ḥilazon for its dye from liability for taking its life?
o: Because taking the life of a snail is never forbidden
Because he has no intent to kill it, and in fact prefers it stay alive longer since live-extracted dye is finer — so the result is not to his benefit
Because the ḥilazon is not considered a living creature
Because Rabbi Yehuda permits it outright
quiz.e: Rava explains this is not a 'cut off its head and it will not die' case of inevitable, desired consequence — the trapper prefers the creature stay alive, so unintentional killing does not create liability here.

quiz.q: According to Rav, why is one who slaughters an animal on Shabbat liable for the labor of DYEING?
o: Because slaughtering always requires dyeing the knife
Because a butcher wants the blood to visibly pool at the slaughtering spot, to attract customers to buy fresh meat
Because animal blood is used to dye cloth
Because this is merely a rabbinic decree with no reason given
quiz.e: Rav explained that the desired outcome of slaughter includes the visible, fresh-dyed appearance of blood, which draws in buyers — making dyeing the relevant melacha.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, who is liable for carrying out of the house an item that people generally do NOT bother to store?
o: No one — such items can never create liability
Only someone who personally stored that particular item, showing he values it
Anyone who carries it, exactly like a normally valuable item
Only the head of the household
quiz.e: The mishna's new principle holds that insignificant items only create carrying-liability for the person who himself designated and stored that specific item, since his action shows it has value to him.
